domain: Reads a 12-bit tile index from an EWRAM map table at 0x02020000 and copies a pair of palette-mapped colour halfwords from a lookup table at 0x02010000 into a VRAM-like destination at 0x06002800 + (a0<<11), writing to two rows 64 bytes apart, walking 11 steps along one axis (the a2-derived row/rowmod pair increments each step; the a1-derived col/colmod/parity values are held fixed for the whole call).
notes: The generated family report clustered this owner with template-main-0801e260 (ui/window/clear_tile_attributes_in_rect.c) at 8259 bp, but the real assembly shares none of that template's tile-attribute-clearing bit logic (no & 0x3FF mask, no RENDER_TILE_ATTR_OFS/RENDER_ALT_OFS access, no |=/&= clear). This is a family-clustering false positive (the n-gram/call-target signal is likely just the common 4-high-register push/pop prologue shared by many owners in this compiler's output), not a genuine template match. The template was not usable as a source-shape starting point for this owner.

Instead this owner's assembly closely matches the CopyEntry idiom already exact in games/gs1/src/map/render_palette_mapped_row.c and render_palette_mapped_column.c: same 0x02010000 colour-table base, same destination-row-doubling pattern (write, then write again 64 bytes later), same '(value/2) & mask' coarse index plus 'value & even-mask' fine destination-offset idiom. This owner appears to be a third sibling in that family (a block/run variant taking two coordinate-like parameters a1,a2 plus a bank selector a0), which is a genuinely useful lead for a future attempt, independent of the assigned template.

The retained candidate (this file) reconstructs the full three-parameter, 11-iteration loop with the CopyBlock(map, destination, parity) static helper and matches the reference instruction-for-instruction for the first 29 instructions (matched_prefix=29 in candidate-show --align) -- the entire parameter-decomposition prologue (sign-correcting halving of a1 and a2, the &0x7F coarse masks, the &30 fine masks, and the a1&1 parity bit) is byte-identical.

The remaining 41 differing halfwords are concentrated in two places: (1) the two wrap-around masks 0x3F80 and 0x3C0 used to re-mask 'row' and 'rowmod' after each += in the loop -- the reference materializes each via movs #imm8; lsls #N (e.g. movs r4,#254; lsls r4,r4,#6), while every source spelling tried here (bare hex literal, and a shift-of-immediate expression '254 << 6') makes this compiler emit a pc-relative ldr from the literal pool instead; and (2) the loop-invariant 0x02020000 map-table base, which the reference reloads from the literal pool on every iteration but which this candidate's compiler hoists into a callee-saved register outside the loop (changing several surrounding instructions to register+register indexed addressing instead of register+immediate).

rejected_experiments.result: worse in both forms (86 and 92 differing halfwords respectively, candidate grew past 172 bytes) -- naming the masks as locals moves their materialization inside the loop body for this compiler instead of hoisting them out, which is worse than the bare-literal version's placement even though neither reaches the reference's movs+lsls encoding.

rejected_experiments.experiment: 2026-08-27 root-cause identification: with the current (retained) candidate, sl/r8 -- the two callee-saved registers the reference dedicates to caching the row/rowmod wrap masks (0x3F80/0x3C0) across all 11 iterations via one-time movs+lsls before the loop plus 'mov rX,sl'/'mov rX,r8' at each iteration's tail -- are instead spent by this compiler on caching two DIFFERENT loop-invariant values: the 0x02020000 map-table base (loaded once via ldr-literal before the loop, reused via register+register indexed addressing each iteration) and the 0xFFF mask used by CopyBlock's '*map & 0xFFF' (also loaded once via ldr-literal, reused via 'ands' each iteration). Because sl/r8 are committed to those two values instead, the row/rowmod masks have no cached register left and get freshly re-materialized via movs+lsls INSIDE the loop body every iteration (dead work, but this compiler's cost heuristic still finds it cheaper than a third high-register live range). This is a global register-allocation PRIORITY difference in which two of the loop's several loop-invariant constants win the two available high-register caching slots, not a local scheduling or expression-shape issue in the row/rowmod computation itself.

2026-08-27: rewrite CopyBlock's index computation from '(*map & 0xFFF) * 4 + parity' to the shift-fusion form '((*map << 20) >> 18) + parity' that matches the reference's own lsls#20/lsrs#18 instruction pair (removing the need to materialize the 0xFFF constant at all, hypothesising this would free r8 for the row/rowmod masks)
rejected_experiments.result: worse (55 differing halfwords / 44 wrong instructions) and changed candidate size to 164 bytes (vs the required 172) -- the compiler DID adopt the lsls#20/lsrs#18 pair matching the reference, but literal-pool layout and downstream register assignment shifted globally as a side effect (matched_prefix collapsed from 29 to 5, and the 240/254 mask-materialization order swapped versus the reference). Removing the 0xFFF pressure did not redirect the freed capacity to the row/rowmod masks; it just reshuffled which values get pool-loaded vs which get movs+lsls'd, still leaving the map base on the register-indexed-addressing path. Confirms the residual is not simply 'one live value too many' but a harder-to-steer global allocation decision.

rejected_experiments.experiment: 2026-08-27: change CopyBlock's first parameter from 'u32 *map' (dereferenced inside CopyBlock as '*map') to 'u32 tile' (dereferenced once in the caller as '*map' and passed by value), keeping the '& 0xFFF' masking form
rejected_experiments.result: byte-identical codegen to the retained candidate (41 differing halfwords / 46 wrong instructions, unchanged) -- this compiler already treats the pointer-vs-value calling convention as equivalent here since CopyBlock is fully inlined either way; no register-pressure change resulted.
